headings.title: Introduction to Haematological Physical Assessment
headings.content: Physical examination plays a pivotal role in the comprehensive evaluation of patients presenting with suspected or diagnosed haematological disorders. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding how to systematically inspect and palpate various body systems helps in identifying early clinical signs of blood dyscrasias, such as anemias, leukemias, and coagulopathies. A thorough assessment goes beyond merely recording laboratory values; it connects physiological pathology with observable physical manifestations. Nurses must approach the physical examination with a structured head-to-toe or systematic regional framework, ensuring no subtle sign of systemic disease is missed. Baseline findings established during this assessment guide ongoing nursing care, evaluate the effectiveness of medical interventions, and alert the healthcare team to potential complications like bleeding crises or severe infections. Developing sharp observation skills and mastering palpation techniques are foundational competencies required for safe and effective clinical practice in haematology wards across Nigerian healthcare settings.

headings.title: General Inspection and Vital Signs
headings.content: General inspection and vital sign monitoring provide immediate clues regarding the systemic severity of a haematological condition. During the initial visual sweep, the nurse observes the patient's overall appearance, nutritional status, and level of consciousness. Signs of chronic fatigue, cachexia, or acute distress are common in severe anemias and advanced malignancies like leukemia. Vital signs must be meticulously assessed: tachycardia and tachypnea often compensate for reduced oxygen-carrying capacity in anaemic states, while a high fever indicates underlying neutropenia and potential life-threatening sepsis. Blood pressure changes can reveal volume depletion or hypovolemic shock resulting from acute haemorrhage. Furthermore, noting posture and ease of breathing helps determine if the patient is experiencing tissue hypoxia or respiratory compromise. In busy clinical environments, recognizing these subtle yet critical shifts in vital signs allows nurses to prioritize urgent interventions and escalate care promptly to prevent patient deterioration.

headings.title: Integumentary System: Skin, Hair, and Nails
headings.content: The integumentary system is a primary mirror for haematological health, revealing hallmark signs of anemia, bleeding disorders, and chronic illness. Pallor, best observed in the conjunctiva, nail beds, palmar creases, and mucous membranes, is a classic indicator of decreased hemoglobin or poor peripheral perfusion. Conversely, plethora or ruddy complexion may suggest polycythemia vera. Nurses must carefully inspect the skin for petechiae (tiny pinpoint hemorrhages), purpura, and ecchymoses, which signal thrombocytopenia or coagulation factor defects. Pigmentation changes, such as hyperpigmentation, can accompany conditions like bone marrow failure syndromes. Nail assessment is equally critical; koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) is strongly associated with chronic iron deficiency anemia, a prevalent nutritional concern in tropical regions. Hair texture changes, dryness, and brittle nails also reflect systemic nutritional deficits secondary to underlying blood disorders. Documenting the exact size, distribution, and color of skin lesions provides vital baseline data for tracking disease progression or treatment response.

headings.title: Examination of the Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, and Throat
headings.content: Examining the head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat (HEENT) uncovers localized manifestations of systemic blood disorders. In the eyes, pallor of the palpebral conjunctiva is a reliable visual indicator of anemia, while scleral icterus points toward hemolysis or liver dysfunction associated with hypersplenism. Examination of the oral cavity is crucial; glossitis (a smooth, red, sore tongue) frequently accompanies vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anemias. Furthermore, inspection of the gums may reveal gingival hyperplasia, a well-known feature of acute myeloid leukemia, or spontaneous bleeding and ulceration due to severe neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Epistaxis, or frequent nosebleeds, can be a presenting symptom in clotting disorders or bone marrow suppression. Nurses should use a penlight and tongue depressor carefully to visualize the oropharynx, checking for exudates, petechiae on the soft palate, or mucosal pallor, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation of the upper aerodigestive tract in relation to haematological status.

headings.title: Lymph Node Assessment
headings.content: Lymph node assessment is an essential component of the physical examination, especially when investigating lymphoproliferative disorders such as lymphomas, leukemias, and chronic infections. Nurses must systematically palpate major lymph node chains using the pads of the index and middle fingers in a gentle, circular motion. Key areas to examine include the pre- and post-auricular, occipital, tonsillar, submandibular, submental, anterior and posterior cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal regions. The examiner must note specific characteristics: location, size, shape, delimitation (discrete or matted), consistency (soft, firm, or hard), tenderness, and mobility. Hard, fixed, and non-tender nodes often raise suspicion for malignancy or metastatic disease, whereas tender, soft, and mobile nodes are typically inflammatory or reactive. Supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, in particular, warrants immediate attention as it frequently indicates serious internal pathology. Careful documentation helps clinicians track disease staging and monitor treatment efficacy over time.

headings.title: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Evaluation
headings.content: Cardiovascular and respiratory evaluations are critical because the circulatory and pulmonary systems bear the brunt of altered blood composition. In severe anemia, the heart works harder to deliver adequate oxygen to tissues, frequently resulting in a hyperdynamic state characterized by tachycardia, a bounding pulse, and systolic flow murmurs auscultated over the precordium. Nurses must listen carefully for extra heart sounds, such as an S3 gallop, which can signal early heart failure secondary to chronic cardiac strain. Respiratory assessment focuses on detecting signs of tissue hypoxia and pulmonary congestion. Tachypnea, dyspnea on exertion, and decreased breath sounds may indicate severe anemia, pulmonary hemorrhage in bleeding disorders, or opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients. Auscultation may reveal crackles if fluid overload develops from blood transfusions or impaired cardiac function. Monitoring these cardiorespiratory parameters ensures early detection of cardiopulmonary decompensation, a common and dangerous complication in haematological crises.

headings.title: Abdominal Examination: Hepatomegaly and Splenomegaly
headings.content: Abdominal examination provides vital insights into organs responsible for blood cell production, destruction, and filtration, namely the liver and spleen. Hepatomegaly (enlarged liver) and splenomegaly (enlarged spleen) frequently occur in haematological disorders such as leukemias, lymphomas, hemolytic anemias, and myeloproliferative neoplasms. During assessment, the nurse inspects the abdomen for asymmetry or distension, auscultates bowel sounds, and proceeds with light followed by deep palpation. When palpating the spleen, the nurse begins in the right lower quadrant and moves diagonally toward the left upper quadrant, asking the patient to take a deep breath so the descending spleen meets the examining fingers. An enlarged spleen must be measured in centimeters below the left costal margin, and extreme care should be taken to avoid aggressive palpation, as a massively enlarged spleen is fragile and prone to rupture. Similarly, liver span is percussed and palpated below the right costal margin. Documenting organomegaly helps gauge disease burden and therapeutic response.

headings.title: Musculoskeletal and Neurological Manifestations
headings.content: Musculoskeletal and neurological manifestations often complete the clinical picture of complex haematological conditions. Bone pain, particularly in the sternum, ribs, and vertebrae, is a classic hallmark of multiple myeloma and acute leukemias due to bone marrow expansion and infiltration by malignant cells. Nurses should gently assess for localized bone tenderness upon palpation. Neurological assessments evaluate the impact of vitamin deficiencies, neurotoxic chemotherapy, or central nervous system involvement by malignancy. Peripheral neuropathies, manifested as numbness, tingling, or burning sensations in the extremities, are common in pernicious anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency. Furthermore, severe anemia or intracranial bleeding associated with profound thrombocytopenia can lead to altered mental status, confusion, lethargy, or focal neurological deficits. Conducting a baseline neurological exam ensures timely identification of central nervous system compromise, guiding urgent medical and nursing interventions.
